Good morning, everyone. Thank you for joining this litigation-planning meeting. As you all know, we're defending the company against a former employee's trade secrets misappropriation lawsuit, and the complaint is seeking broad inspection of our devices and systems. We have an initial case-management conference coming up next month, and no discovery has been exchanged yet. The company's priorities are clear: we need to protect our confidential information while keeping defense costs controlled.

Before I approve the initial defense plan, I need each of you to identify any facts or considerations that should shape our approach. Discovery counsel, I want to hear from you on what you're seeing on the discovery front. Insurance-coverage counsel, I need to understand where we stand on coverage for this matter. Let's get everything on the table so we can build a plan that addresses the real issues.

transcript.text: Elena, I need to flag several coverage facts that will directly shape our defense plan. I've reviewed the applicable policy endorsement, and here's what it provides: First, the trade-secret defense is covered, but subject to a $75,000 self-insured retention. Second, we must use insurer-approved panel counsel. Third, we need written insurer consent before engaging any forensic vendor — this is critical given the broad device and system inspection the complaint seeks. Fourth, we are required to notify the insurer as part of the approved defense plan. I should note that the endorsement itself is stored in the risk department's file and has not yet been attached to this matter. These requirements need to be built into our plan now, before we make any commitments on counsel selection or forensic engagement.

My forensic review of the former employee's company laptop has been completed, and the findings are significant for our defense strategy. The review confirmed that exactly three identified trade-secret files were copied to the device. Critically, the review found no customer data on the device and no evidence of any additional copying beyond those three files. This substantially narrows the scope of what the plaintiff can reasonably seek through broad device and system inspection. However, I should note that my forensic report is still awaiting final partner review and has not yet been added to the case plan. This information should shape our approach at the case-management conference — we can push back on the broad inspection demands by demonstrating that the actual scope of copying is limited and identifiable. That said, given Morgan's point about needing insurer consent before engaging forensic vendors, we should discuss how to align this completed work with the coverage requirements.

We need to understand whether this forensic work was done through a vendor or internally, and if through a vendor, whether insurer consent was obtained beforehand. If not, there could be coverage implications we need to address proactively with the insurer. Elena, I'd recommend we resolve this question before finalizing the defense plan, because it affects both our coverage position and how we can use these findings at the case-management conference. The good news is that the narrow scope Samir describes — three identified files, no customer data, no additional copying — could actually support our argument to the insurer that the forensic engagement was reasonable and necessary. But we need to get ahead of this rather than discovering a coverage gap later.

decisions.discovery_scope: Limited to the three identified trade-secret files on the former employee's company laptop; oppose broad device and system inspection demands based on forensic findings showing no customer data and no additional copying
decisions.counsel_model: Insurer-approved panel counsel, consistent with policy endorsement requirements

commitments.detail: Confirm whether insurer consent was obtained for the completed forensic review of the former employee's laptop, and if not, proactively notify the insurer and seek retroactive approval, emphasizing the reasonable and necessary nature of the engagement given the narrow scope of findings.
Obtain and attach the policy endorsement from the risk department's file to this matter, and submit the approved defense plan to the insurer with written notification as required.
Obtain final partner review of the forensic report and add it to the case plan so the findings can be used to support our opposition to broad discovery at the case-management conference.
